title: MacBook Ultra: Everything Apple Is Reportedly Planning
summary: Apple is reportedly planning a major MacBook redesign dubbed the "MacBook Ultra": an OLED, touchscreen clamshell with a thinner chassis and smaller notch arriving around late 2026–early 2027. Initial models may ship with M5 Pro and M5 Max silicon, with M7-class chips coming later, and higher pricing than current Pros. Memory supply issues could delay mass production.

Apple’s first OLED MacBook with a touchscreen and Dynamic Island could arrive late 2026, starting at $2,499.

Key Takeaways

Apple is reportedly preparing a major Mac laptop overhaul that some sources call the "MacBook Ultra." Multiple reports, including coverage by MacRumors and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, describe an OLED-touchscreen machine that could land in late 2026 or slip into early 2027 depending on global memory supply constraints.

The marquee rumor centers on the display. Apple is said to plan using tandem OLED technology — the same approach used in the iPad Pro — promising deeper contrast, richer color, and better power efficiency than current mini-LED panels. Paired with that screen would be Apple’s first-ever Mac touchscreen, framed as "touch-friendly, not touch-first." The design remains a clamshell: no folding, no detaching, just a touchscreen that responds to touch when you want it to.

Other expected design changes include a thinner chassis, a disappearing or diminished notch, and slightly thinner bezels on both 14-inch and 16-inch models, according to display industry tracking.

On silicon, the picture is more nuanced. Multiple reports indicate the first redesigned models may ship with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips — the same families currently available in existing MacBook Pros — while next-generation M7-class silicon would be reserved for a later refresh around late 2027. That means early buyers would be paying a premium for the revamped design and display rather than for a performance leap.

Pricing and timing are intertwined. The new device is positioned above the existing Pro line and is expected to command a higher price. Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo has suggested mass production could begin in late 2026, but ongoing memory chip shortages make early 2027 more likely for many shipments.

For buyers, the decision depends on priorities. If OLED quality, a touchscreen, and the revised industrial design matter most, waiting could be worthwhile. If raw compute performance is the priority, current MacBook Pro models already use the chips rumored for the initial redesign and may represent better value today.

Context and caveats: these are industry reports and rumors; features, timing, and pricing are subject to change, especially given supply-chain volatility. Apple has not confirmed these details.

Editorial note: This summary is drawn from reporting aggregated by technology outlets and analysts. Gadget Review notes its editorial process blends human expertise with AI-assisted refinement to deliver clear, concise coverage.

For anyone weighing aMacBookPro purchase right now, one rumor deserves a pause. Apple is reportedly preparing its most significant Mac laptop overhaul in years — a device some sources call the“MacBook Ultra,”according toMacRumors. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman describes an OLED-touchscreen machine that could landlate 2026or slip into early 2027, depending on a global memory chip shortage that keeps pushing timelines. The question isn’t whether this sounds impressive. It’s whether waiting makes sense for your wallet and your work.

The first OLED Mac would bring a touchscreen, a thinner chassis, and a disappearing notch — but none of the iPad-style convertible tricks you might expect.

The marquee rumor is the display. Apple reportedly plans to usetandemOLEDtechnology— the same approach powering the iPad Pro — delivering deeper contrast, richer color, and better power efficiency than today’s mini-LED panels. Paired with that screen is Apple’s first-ever Mac touchscreen,framed by Gurman as“touch-friendly, not touch-first.” No folding. No detaching. Just a clamshell that responds to your finger when you want it to.

Several other rumored features round out the redesign:

Earlier reports pointed to next-generation silicon, but current sourcing suggests you might pay a premium for chips already on sale today.

Here’s where the pitch gets complicated. Multiple reports now indicate the first redesign ships withM5 Proand M5 Max — the same chips sitting inside today’s MacBook Pro. The more powerful M7-class silicon is reportedly reserved for a later refresh around late 2027. Think of it like buying a beautifully renovated apartment that still runs on last year’s HVAC system: you’re paying for the architecture, not a performance ceiling.

That framing matters when you factor in pricing:

This positions the device firmly above the existing Pro line. AnalystMing-Chi Kuoreportedly sees mass production beginning late 2026, though memory supply constraints make early 2027 the more realistic window. Both 14-inch and 16-inch sizes should feature slightly thinner bezels, per display industry tracker Omdia.

If OLED quality and touch interaction matter most to your workflow, the wait may well be worth it. If raw performance is the priority, the current MacBook Pro already runs the same chips you’d reportedly get in the redesign — at alower price.
